Sleep Regression Ages: 4, 8, 12 and 18 Month Guide

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sleep regressions most often happen around 4 months, 8 to 10 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 2 years, and each one typically lasts two to six weeks. A regression is a temporary stretch when a baby who was sleeping better suddenly wakes more at night or fights naps, usually alongside a burst of development. It is a parent term, not a medical diagnosis, and it almost always passes. This guide walks through each age, what drives it, and how to respond without creating new problems.

What a sleep regression is and how to spot one

A sleep regression is a temporary rough patch, usually two to six weeks, when a baby who had settled into a decent rhythm starts waking more at night, fighting naps, or resisting bedtime. The word regression sounds alarming, but nothing is going backward. These stretches almost always line up with a leap in development: a new motor skill, a language burst, or a change in how your baby experiences separation. Sleep is often the first thing to wobble when the brain is busy. Regression is a term parents and sleep coaches use, not a diagnosis your pediatrician will make, and it does not mean you did anything wrong.

The signs of a sleep regression are usually sudden and clustered. A baby who slept long stretches starts waking every hour or two. Naps shrink to twenty minutes or get skipped. Bedtime turns into a protest, and your baby may be clingier or fussier during the day while practicing something new, like rolling or pulling to stand. Appetite and mood are otherwise normal, which is one useful clue that this is development rather than illness. Jot down the date it started somewhere you will find again. Knowing you are two weeks in, not two months, makes the hard nights easier to ride out.

The 4 month regression: the one true reset

Around 3 to 5 months, babies permanently outgrow newborn sleep. Instead of drifting into deep sleep quickly, they begin cycling through lighter and deeper stages the way older children and adults do, surfacing briefly between cycles. This is a maturation of the brain, not a phase that reverses, which is why the 4 month regression feels different from the others. A baby who used to be fed or rocked into a deep sleep now half-wakes every sleep cycle and notices that the situation has changed: no arms, no bottle, no motion. Each of those surfacings can become a full waking with a call for help.

Because the change is lasting, the way through is helping your baby get comfortable with the new sleep pattern rather than waiting for the old sleep to return. Put your baby down drowsy but awake for at least one sleep a day so falling asleep starts to happen in the crib. Keep the room dark, keep a short consistent wind-down, and give it time. Many families ride this stage out with extra support at night and revisit habits later. If wakings stay frequent after several weeks and everyone is exhausted, that is a reasonable moment to read up on gentle settling methods, which our sleep training guide covers in detail.

Later regressions: 8 months to 2 years

The 8 to 10 month regression usually arrives with big motor skills and big feelings. Babies who are learning to crawl, sit up, or pull to stand often practice in the crib, sometimes getting stuck standing and crying for help. Separation anxiety also tends to ramp up in this window, so being put down and left can suddenly feel like a much bigger deal. Around 12 months, walking, first words, and a growing will can stir sleep again. Some 1 year olds also start refusing the morning nap for a week or two. That protest is usually temporary, and most children genuinely need two naps a while longer.

The 18 month regression tends to be driven by independence and language. Toddlers this age are discovering that they have opinions, and bedtime is a natural place to test them. Separation anxiety can flare again, and first molars sometimes overlap, which muddies the picture. Around age 2, sleep can wobble because of nighttime fears, a later bedtime fight, or life changes like a new sibling, toilet learning, or the tempting idea of a big kid bed. Through all of these, the same rule holds: the cause is developmental, the disruption is temporary, and calm consistent responses shorten it. Most toddlers settle back within a few weeks.

Regression, teething, illness, or a nap problem?

Teething and regressions get blamed for the same nights, but they look different up close. Teething discomfort is usually worst in the few days around a tooth breaking through, and it comes with daytime clues: heavy drooling, gnawing, a tender swollen spot on the gum, and fussiness that eases with comfort. A regression runs longer, comes with new skills or clinginess rather than gum signs, and the daytime mood is often fine. Illness is its own category. Fever, ear pulling or rubbing, a change in feeding, unusual crying, or a baby who simply seems sick warrants a call to your pediatrician rather than a wait and see plan.

A mistimed nap schedule can also masquerade as a regression. A baby who is dropping a nap, or being pushed to drop one too early, may fight bedtime, wake overnight, or rise early because daytime sleep pressure no longer matches the schedule. If the disruption built gradually rather than appearing overnight, and there is no new skill or clingy phase to point to, look at the nap schedule first. Our guide to nap transitions walks through the usual ages and how to adjust. Early morning waking has its own set of causes and fixes, and we cover those separately as well.

How to respond, and when to call your pediatrician

Hold the routine steady. Keep the same bedtime, the same order of steps, and the same sleep space, because familiarity is what your baby anchors to while everything else is changing. Give the new skill plenty of daytime practice so the crib is not the only gym available at 2 a.m. At night, keep checks brief and boring: a low voice, a hand on the chest, minimal light, then out. Comfort freely, but be thoughtful about starting new habits, like a return to feeding to sleep, that you may have to unwind in a few weeks, and skip bed sharing entirely: for babies under 12 months, the safest place to sleep is their own crib or bassinet on a firm, flat surface. It can help to note start dates and wake times in BeMama or a notebook so you can see the pattern instead of guessing.

Call your pediatrician if sleep disruption comes with snoring, noisy breathing, or pauses in breathing, with fever, ear pulling, or other signs of illness, or if feeding and weight are a concern. If your baby ever stops breathing, goes limp, or turns blue or gray, that is an emergency: call 911 rather than waiting for an appointment. Also check in if the disruption lasts beyond about six weeks, because at that point something other than a regression may be keeping it going. And if sleep loss is dragging your own mood, safety, or ability to function down, say so at the visit; that matters too. Once a regression has clearly passed but the extra wakings have stuck around as habit, our sleep training guide can help you reset gently.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Sleep patterns change with development, illness, travel, separation anxiety, and nap transitions. Consistent wake times, calming routines, age-appropriate naps, and a safe sleep environment are more useful than expecting one universal schedule.

Behavioral sleep approaches should fit the child’s age, temperament, feeding needs, health, and family values. Persistent snoring, breathing pauses, pain, poor growth, or extreme daytime sleepiness needs clinical assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to compare sleep patterns and routines across days. Totals cannot diagnose a sleep disorder or determine that a sleep arrangement is safe.

When to seek help

Continue infant safe-sleep practices for babies. Seek medical advice for breathing concerns, unusual sleepiness, poor feeding, or a sudden major change.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Separation Anxiety & Sleeping Trouble in Young Children
  • CDC — Positive Parenting Tips: Toddlers (2–3 years old)
  • Public Health Agency of Canada — Safe Sleep for Your Baby

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Sleep regressions cluster around 4 months, 8 to 10 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 2 years.
  • Most regressions last about two to six weeks and pass on their own.
  • The 4 month regression is a lasting change in sleep cycles, so help your baby learn to settle rather than waiting it out.
  • Keep the bedtime routine identical, keep night checks brief and boring, and avoid new habits you will have to unwind.
  • Call your pediatrician for snoring, breathing pauses, fever, ear pulling, or disruption lasting beyond six weeks.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a sleep regression last?

Most sleep regressions last about two to six weeks. The rough patch usually eases once the new skill is mastered or the developmental leap settles. If disrupted sleep drags on past six weeks, look for another cause, such as a nap schedule that needs adjusting or wakings that have become habit, and mention it at your next pediatric visit.

What are the signs of a sleep regression?

The main signs are a sudden increase in night wakings, shorter or skipped naps, and new resistance at bedtime in a baby who had been sleeping better. Daytime clinginess and intense practice of a new skill, like rolling or standing, often appear at the same time. Appetite and mood are usually otherwise normal, which helps separate a regression from illness.

Is it a sleep regression or teething?

It is more likely teething if the disruption is brief, peaks in the few days around a tooth coming through, and comes with drooling, gnawing, and a swollen gum. A regression lasts longer, weeks rather than days, and pairs with new skills or separation worries instead of gum signs. Fever or ear pulling points to illness rather than teething, so call your pediatrician if you see either.

Is the 4 month sleep regression real, and does it end?

Yes, it is real, and the rough patch does end, but the change behind it is permanent. Around 3 to 5 months, babies shift to mature sleep cycles with brief wakings between them, and that pattern is here to stay. Sleep improves once your baby learns to link cycles with less help, which is why practicing settling works better than waiting for old sleep to come back.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
